title: Narrative Review Details Saudi Arabia Pediatric Respiratory Syncytial Virus Burden - Bioengineer.org

analysis.time: The review was published on November 23, 2026. The event dates referenced include the autumn and winter months, with peak intensity during December and January, and lowest circulation during the summer months (June through August).
analysis.location_and_population: The review focuses on Saudi Arabia, particularly Riyadh and Jazan, with data from the Eastern Province. It examines pediatric populations aged eighteen years or younger, including infants under two years and children under twelve months.
analysis.event: A comprehensive narrative review published in the Journal of Infection and Public Health details the burden of respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) in Saudi Arabia, highlighting its role in pediatric respiratory morbidity and hospital admissions. The review is based on observational investigations, hospital-based surveillance reports, molecular genotyping studies, and health-economic models.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: RSV was detected in 28.9 percent of 1,429 screened children in Riyadh, accounting for 79.1 percent of all virus-positive samples in that cohort. In an 885-patient tertiary cohort in Riyadh, 60.3 percent of confirmed pediatric patients required hospital admission, with 26.2 percent needing intensive care support and an overall mortality rate of 2.4 percent. In Jazan, 31.8 percent of hospitalized cases were admitted to intensive care, with a mortality rate of 8.7 percent.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The authors manually screened publications and cross-checked extracted clinical settings, observation periods, diagnostic methods, seasonal patterns, and economic parameters against primary sources. They opted for a narrative synthesis rather than statistical pooling due to heterogeneity in regional study denominators, clinical case selection, and diagnostic protocols. The review also discusses the potential impact of emerging monoclonal antibodies and maternal immunization regimens on future infant disease prevention.

analysis.brief_en: A comprehensive narrative review published in the Journal of Infection and Public Health highlights the significant burden of respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) in Saudi Arabia, particularly among young infants. The review, conducted by researchers Ammar A. Alabdali, Chu Guat Yeap, and Thamir A. Alandijany, synthesizes observational studies, hospital-based surveillance, molecular genotyping, and health-economic models to assess RSV's impact on pediatric respiratory health. The findings indicate that RSV is a major cause of hospital admissions, with detection rates ranging from 20 to 30 percent in general pediatric cohorts. In Riyadh, 28.9 percent of 1,429 screened children under five tested positive for RSV, accounting for 79.1 percent of all virus-positive samples. In an 885-patient tertiary cohort, 60.3 percent of confirmed cases required hospital admission, with 26.2 percent needing intensive care and an overall mortality rate of 2.4 percent. In Jazan, 31.8 percent of hospitalized cases were admitted to intensive care, with a mortality rate of 8.7 percent. The authors emphasize that variations in detection rates are linked to clinical severity and testing criteria rather than geographic differences. They also note that young age, especially under twelve months, is the primary determinant of severe disease and hospitalization. The review underscores the need for continued genomic tracking of RSV-B isolates, as monoclonal antibodies targeting specific epitopes are being developed for broader use. The study highlights the seasonal nature of RSV, with peak activity between December and January and lower circulation during the summer months (June through August).

analysis.time: The study was conducted across three epidemic seasons between 2018 and 2025, with the 2024–2025 season being the first under systematic public health recommendations for universal infant RSV prophylaxis. The publication date of the report is November 19, 2026.

The analysis included children from the Berlin metropolitan area, with the hospital accounting for 33% of RSV-related hospitalizations in 2023–2024 and 25.6% in 2024–2025.
analysis.event: A retrospective observational investigation at the Children’s Hospital of Charité – Universitätsklinikum Berlin showed that pediatric hospital admissions for respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) decreased by fifty-one percent following the nationwide implementation of passive immunization with nirsevimab. The study also noted that more than ninety percent of hospitalized infants during the 2024–2025 season had not received nirsevimab.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: RSV hospitalizations in the tertiary center dropped by 44% compared to the 2018–2019 season and 51% compared to the 2023–2024 season. The nationwide reduction was estimated at 55%, with almost one hundred thousand pediatric hospitalizations documented in Germany between 2019 and 2022. The study highlights the significant seasonal strain on pediatric healthcare infrastructure due to RSV.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The study was conducted as a retrospective observational investigation, with findings based on hospital records and laboratory confirmation via polymerase chain reaction or rapid antigen testing. The results are supported by the Robert Koch Institute and the Federal Ministry of Health, but the report notes methodological constraints that limit direct interpretation of the findings.

analysis.brief_en: A study conducted at the Children’s Hospital of Charité – Universitätsklinikum Berlin in Germany found that the introduction of nirsevimab, a monoclonal antibody, led to a 51% reduction in infant RSV hospitalizations during the 2024–2025 season. This marked decrease followed the national recommendation for passive immunization issued by the Standing Committee on Vaccination (STIKO) in 2024. The research analyzed 261 hospitalized children under two years of age across three epidemic seasons (2018–2019, 2023–2024, and 2024–2025), revealing that 90.2% of infants hospitalized with RSV during the 2024–2025 season had not received the antibody. The study also noted that the Charité center accounted for 33% of RSV-related hospitalizations in the Berlin metropolitan area during 2023–2024 and 25.6% during 2024–2025, aligning with the nationwide 55% reduction reported by the Robert Koch Institute. The findings suggest a strong correlation between nirsevimab uptake and reduced acute healthcare utilization, though the report acknowledges methodological limitations in interpreting the results. The study underscores the significant seasonal burden of RSV on pediatric healthcare systems and highlights the potential impact of prophylactic measures.
